title: 3Sum — sort + fix one + two-pointer scan, skip duplicates.
shortTitle: 3Sum — Sort + Fix One + Two-Pointer, Skip Duplicates

s1_definition.profdef: The 3Sum problem finds all unique triples in an array that sum to a target, typically zero. The standard solution first sorts the array, then fixes one element and uses the two-pointer technique on the remaining sorted range to find pairs that complete the triple, moving a left and right pointer inward based on whether the current sum is too small or too large, while skipping duplicate values to avoid repeated triples. Sorting is N log N and the nested two-pointer scan is quadratic, so the overall time is quadratic with constant extra space beyond the output.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India wants to find every group of three transactions on Rajesh's account that net to zero, meaning they cancel out, because such offsetting triples can signal wash-trading. First the amounts are sorted. Then a clerk fixes one amount and uses two fingers on the rest of the sorted list, one at the low end and one at the high end, moving them toward each other: if the three add to more than zero the high finger steps down, if less the low finger steps up, and if exactly zero the triple is recorded. Duplicate amounts are skipped so the same triple is never reported twice.
s1_definition.oneliner: Sort, fix one element, then two-pointer the rest inward, skipping duplicates to keep triples unique.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The 3Sum problem finds all unique triples in an array that sum to a target, typically zero. The standard solution first sorts the array, then fixes one element and uses the two-pointer technique on the remaining sorted range to find pairs that complete the triple, moving a left and right pointer inward based on whether the current sum is too small or too large, while skipping duplicate values to avoid repeated triples. Sorting is N log N and the nested two-pointer scan is quadratic, so the overall time is quadratic with constant extra space beyond the output.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India wants to find every group of three transactions on Rajesh's account that net to zero, meaning they cancel out, because such offsetting triples can signal wash-trading. First the amounts are sorted. Then a clerk fixes one amount and uses two fingers on the rest of the sorted list, one at the low end and one at the high end, moving them toward each other: if the three add to more than zero the high finger steps down, if less the low finger steps up, and if exactly zero the triple is recorded. Duplicate amounts are skipped so the same triple is never reported twice.

**One line to remember:** Sort, fix one element, then two-pointer the rest inward, skipping duplicates to keep triples unique.

sections.s2_technical:
Sorting first is the enabling step. Once the array is sorted, you can use the two-pointer technique, which relies on order: if a sum is too small you move the left pointer right to increase it, and if too large you move the right pointer left to decrease it. Without sorting you could not reason about which pointer to move.

The outer loop fixes the first element of the triple at index i, moving from the start toward the end. For each fixed element, you set a left pointer just after i and a right pointer at the end. You compute the sum of the fixed element plus the elements at left and right. If the sum equals the target you record the triple, then advance both pointers past any duplicates. If the sum is less than the target you move left rightward; if greater you move right leftward. The inner scan is linear for each fixed element, so the total is quadratic.

Skipping duplicates is the part that makes the triples unique and is the most error-prone detail. There are three places to skip. First, in the outer loop, if the current fixed element equals the previous fixed element, you skip it, because it would regenerate the same triples. Second and third, after recording a valid triple, you advance the left pointer past any equal values and the right pointer past any equal values, so you do not record the same triple again. Getting all three skips right is what distinguishes a correct solution from one that emits duplicates.

A senior point is an early-exit optimisation. Because the array is sorted, once the fixed element is greater than the target, and the target is zero, no triple can sum to zero since the remaining elements are all at least as large, so you can break out of the outer loop. This prunes a lot of work on arrays with many positives.

Another senior point is why this beats the brute force. The naive triple nested loop is cubic, which is far too slow for large inputs. The sort plus two-pointer reduces it to quadratic, which is the accepted optimal for comparison-based 3Sum. A hash-based approach also exists but managing duplicates with hashing is fiddlier, so the sort plus two-pointer is the cleaner standard.

For finance I use BigDecimal and compareTo, and I collect triples into a list of lists. I note that sorting BigDecimal uses natural order, and duplicate skipping uses compareTo equal to zero so scale differences do not create spurious distinct values.

A small finance-domain example sketch: sort the amounts, then `for i: if (i>0 && a[i]==a[i-1]) continue; int l=i+1, r=n-1; while (l<r) { cmp sum vs target; on equal record and skip dups; else move l or r; }` collects all unique zero-sum triples.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India surveillance team looks for sets of three transactions on Rajesh's account whose signed amounts net to zero, because offsetting triples where credits and debits cancel can indicate wash-trading used to fake activity. They must find all unique such triples efficiently across a day's transactions. Finding all zero-sum triples with sort plus two-pointer is exactly this.

This is exactly how 3Sum works in Java — sort the amounts, fix one, and two-pointer the rest to find completing pairs, skipping duplicates.

Problem 2 — A day can contain duplicate amounts, and the team must not see the same offsetting triple reported many times, so the duplicate-skipping at all three points is essential, and amounts are BigDecimal so comparisons and duplicate checks use compareTo. This shows mastery of the uniqueness handling and the money data type.

What the code will do: a `WashTradeDetector` with `zeroSumTriples(BigDecimal[] amounts)` that sorts a copy, fixes one, two-pointers the rest, and skips duplicates at all three points. The demo scans a day of signed amounts and logs the unique offsetting triples.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: the signed amounts are `-1000, -1000, 500, 500, 1000, 0`.

Step 1: We copy and sort the amounts to `-1000, -1000, 0, 500, 500, 1000`, leaving the original untouched. n is six.

Step 2: Fix i at index zero, value `-1000`. It is not a duplicate of a previous element and is not greater than zero, so we proceed. left is one, right is five.

Step 3: Sum is `-1000 + (-1000) + 1000 = -1000`, which is less than zero, so we move left right to index two. Sum is `-1000 + 0 + 1000 = 0`, exactly zero, so we record the triple `-1000, 0, 1000`. We then skip duplicates: left advances past the `0`, right steps down past the `1000`.

Step 4: Now left is three with `500` and right is four with `500`. Sum is `-1000 + 500 + 500 = 0`, exactly zero, so we record the triple `-1000, 500, 500`. We skip duplicates: left advances past both `500` values, which crosses right, so the inner loop ends.

Step 5: Fix i at index one, value `-1000` again. This equals the previous fixed element, so we skip it to avoid regenerating the same triples. This is the first duplicate-skip point in action.

Step 6: Fix i at index two, value `0`. It is greater than the target zero? No, it equals zero, so we continue, but the two-pointer finds no new zero-sum triple beyond what was found, and once the fixed element would exceed zero the early exit stops the outer loop. The result holds two unique triples, with no duplicates despite the repeated amounts, and the original array is unchanged.

Final output:

```
2026-10-26T18:00:00Z INFO Found 2 zero-sum triples
2026-10-26T18:00:00Z INFO Unique offsetting triples: [[-1000, 0, 1000], [-1000, 500, 500]]
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Input: [-1000,-1000,500,500,1000,0]
    │
    ▼
  sort copy → [-1000,-1000,0,500,500,1000]
    │
    ▼
  fix i=0 (-1000), two-pointer l,r inward
    │ sum<0 → l++  ; sum==0 → record & skip dups ; sum>0 → r--
    │ records: [-1000,0,1000], [-1000,500,500]
    │ fix i=1 (-1000) == prev → SKIP (dup fixed)
    │ fix i>=0 value>0 → early break
    ▼
  [[-1000,0,1000],[-1000,500,500]]  (unique)
    ▼
  Output: offsetting triples flagged for surveillance
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
3Sum finds all unique triples that sum to a target, usually zero, and the standard solution is sort plus two-pointer. I sort the array first, which lets me use the two-pointer technique: for each fixed first element I put a left pointer just after it and a right pointer at the end, and I move them inward based on the sum, raising it by moving left right when the sum is too small and lowering it by moving right left when too large, recording a triple when the sum hits the target. Sorting is N log N and the nested scan is quadratic, so the whole thing is quadratic, which is the accepted optimal and far better than the cubic brute force.

The part I am most careful about is skipping duplicates at three points: skip a fixed element equal to the previous one, and after recording a triple advance the left pointer past equal values and the right pointer past equal values. Those three skips are what keep the triples unique, and missing any of them produces repeated triples.

I also use the early-exit optimisation: because the array is sorted, once the fixed element exceeds the target of zero no triple can sum to zero, so I break out of the outer loop, which prunes a lot of work on arrays with many positives. For money I sort BigDecimal in natural order and use compareTo for both the sum comparison and the duplicate checks so that scale differences do not create spurious distinct values, and I sort a copy to leave the caller's array untouched.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India I used this in wash-trade surveillance to find all unique sets of three transactions whose signed amounts net to zero, because offsetting triples where credits and debits cancel can indicate faked activity. Days contain duplicate amounts, so the three duplicate-skips ensure each offsetting triple is reported once. Explaining the sort-enabled two-pointer, the three duplicate-skip points, and the early exit shows the interviewer that I know the optimal 3Sum and the uniqueness handling that trips most candidates.
